# Your Java 8 App Still Ships. That's the Security Problem.

It's not Java 6. It's Java 8. The app still makes money. The team still ships. And every quarter someone asks when you're "going to modernize."

Modernize is a vague word. Through a security and testing lens it means something sharper: can you still get patches, can you still prove TLS and crypto aren't stuck on defaults that aged out from under you, and do you have tests that catch the upgrade breakage before production does?

## What "still on Java 8" actually means for patches

Oracle's [Java SE Support Roadmap](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/java-se-support-roadmap.html) (updated August 4, 2026) is blunt about timelines.

For Oracle Java SE 8 (LTS):

- Premier Support ran through **March 2022**
- Extended Support runs through **December 2030**
- Sustaining Support is listed as indefinite

That table is for **Oracle Customers** — people with an active Java SE subscription or equivalent entitlement. Separately, Oracle says free public updates for Personal, Development, and other Users continue indefinitely via java.com, with at least 18 months' notice if that ever ends.

If your production JVM is commercial and nobody is paying for updates, you are not on a free hobby timeline. You are on a "hope nothing critical lands" timeline. Hope is not a patch process.

## The upgrade is not a version bump. It's an inventory.

Oracle's migration docs tell you to start with dependency reality, not a pep-talk slide.

`jdeps` (Java Dependency Analysis) is a JDK tool that shows what packages and classes your app and libraries actually depend on. Oracle's [Preparing for Migration](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/migrate/preparing-migration.html) guide says to run it — including `-jdkinternals` — to find calls into unsupported JDK internal APIs that can break when you move past 8.

Two facts that matter in a real codebase:

1. Internal APIs can be removed or changed incompatibly. That is the point of the warning.
2. `jdeps` is **static**. If something uses reflection to call an internal API, `jdeps` will not warn you. Your tests have to.

Oracle's [JDK 17 migration guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/migrate/getting-started.html) also says to check removed APIs, tools, and components before you start. Skipping that step is how "we'll just bump the JDK in CI" turns into a three-week outage story.

## TLS defaults are part of the same story

Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the protocol that encrypts HTTPS traffic. OWASP's [Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html) says web apps must default to TLS 1.3 and may support TLS 1.2 for compatibility. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated (RFC 8996, March 2021) and must be disabled. They are also called out as forbidden by PCI DSS and disallowed by NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2.

A legacy Java 8 stack that still negotiates old protocols because "a partner needs it" is not a cute compatibility footnote. It is an attack surface you chose to keep open. Isolate EOL clients on a dedicated endpoint with no sensitive data — do not weaken the primary endpoint. That is OWASP's guidance, not a blog opinion.

Same cheat sheet: keep cryptographic libraries patched. Heartbleed-class library bugs are why "we only upgrade the app JAR" is incomplete. The runtime and the crypto stack travel together.

## Testing is the migration, not the afterparty

If you treat tests as something you write after the upgrade PR merges, you will learn your breakage in production.

Minimum bar for a Java 8 → modern LTS move (11 is not the finish line; pick a supported LTS and plan the next hop):

1. **Inventory** with `jdeps` / `-jdkinternals`, plus a dependency CVE scan of the libraries that only exist because the old stack stuck around.
2. **Regression suite that already fails closed** on auth, session, and TLS negotiation before you touch the JDK.
3. **Prove protocol and cipher policy** after the bump — not by eyeballing a screenshot, by automated checks against the policy you claim.
4. **Assume reflection and native bits will surprise you.** Static analysis will miss them. Integration tests that hit real login, file, and crypto paths will not.

You are not modernizing for vanity metrics. You are buying the ability to apply security fixes without a hero weekend.
